genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the central figure looks after the animals of a shelter
she is inside the enclosure before the sky lightens
she likens her trade to that of an interpreter
a thick-coated mammal states its needs differently from a bird
she bottle-feeds the infants left without a mother
she keeps her distance when a grown animal is hurt
she compares her patience to that of someone who works a plot of ground
her colleagues credit her with sensing pain before any visible sign
she puts that reputation down to close and repeated watching
text: The keeper is inside the enclosure before the sky has begun to lighten, a bucket of seed wedged against her hip. Her trade, she says, comes closest to an interpreter's: she listens to tongues that carry no words. A shaggy mammal rubbing itself along the fence is asking for one thing; a bird beating its wings behind glass is asking for something else entirely. The newborns whose mothers have vanished she feeds from a bottle. The wounded grown ones she leaves alone, watching from the far side of the gate. Patience of this kind belongs to anyone who works a plot of ground: healing cannot be hurried, only kept company. Her colleagues swear she senses pain long before the animal starts to limp. She laughs at that, and says she only looks harder, and more often, and without any hurry at all.

units: the piece assesses a film devoted to wildlife
the assessment falls into three aspects
the steadiness of the long takes is judged excellent
one sequence follows a bird of prey settling on a branch
the added music covers the sound recorded on site
the commentary confuses two different bodily states
one passage shows young just taken off the teat
that passage is held to be the best in the film
the crew did not state how long the watching sessions lasted
text: The wildlife film shown last week is worth judging under three headings. The picture first: the long takes are held with a steadiness that never falters, and the camera follows a bird of prey right down onto its branch without a tremor in the frame. The sound is another matter. A layer of added music keeps swallowing what the recordists caught on the spot, the shifting of leaves, the settling of feathers. Then the science: the commentary runs together two distinct states, the deep torpor of a winter sleeper and the light dozing of a beast that wakes at intervals, and an argument otherwise well built is weakened by it. What redeems the whole is the passage on the young just taken off the teat, where gestures pass from one generation to the next. A pity the crew never said how long they watched.

units: the letter is addressed to a woman living in the house next door
it concerns a ginger cat that moves from one plot to the other
the writer saw it at dusk hidden under a hedge
the animal was watching birds that had come to drink
the next day it settled on a window ledge
the writer first supposed it belonged to a tenant
the worn collar and the thinness of the animal changed her mind
she gives it water but will not feed it
the animal walks badly on a hind limb
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about the ginger cat that moves back and forth between our two gardens. Last week, at dusk, I caught sight of him under the hedge, flattened low, watching the birds that come to drink at the stone basin. The following morning he crossed the low wall and settled on my window ledge. My first thought was that he belonged to the tenant at the far end, until I noticed how worn his collar was and how thin he had grown. Since then I have been putting out fresh water for him, though I have stopped short of feeding him, so as not to tie him to my yard. Should you know who owns him, I should be grateful if you would pass the word on: he is walking badly on one hind leg. I am glad to discuss the matter in person. Yours sincerely, the tenant of the house alongside.

units: the wall of the egg grows thinner from the inside
the embryo draws off the calcium meant for its skeleton
a longer incubation yields a more finished young one
that young one moves about as soon as it leaves the shell
other species are born without feathers and without sight
this strategy shortens the time the female stays still over the clutch
it therefore lowers the risk of being spotted by a hunter
the adults must then feed young that cannot move
neither strategy is presented as the better one
text: What goes on inside an egg in the last hours before hatching? The shell grows thinner from within, because the embryo is drawing off the calcium its own skeleton needs. Why does one chick come out in thick down and another with bare skin? It rests on how long the incubation lasts: the longer the wait, the more finished the chick, and some are on their feet and running the moment the shell gives way. So what does a species gain by hatching its young naked and blind? It cuts short the stretch of days when the female must sit motionless over the clutch, and with that it lowers her chances of being marked by anything out hunting. The bill comes later, since the parents must then feed mouths that cannot move. Does one method win, then? Neither does. Each answers the pressures of its own surroundings.

units: someone from the neighbourhood tells of his troubles with livestock
his rabbits were digging under the fence and getting out
the runaways headed for the vegetable patch at the bottom
the man had already sunk the wire netting deeper
the animals were slipping through a gap he had not found
his daughter suggests laying a wide board flat against the fence
a digging animal starts its hole at the foot of the obstacle
it gives up when it meets a hard surface
the family nailed boards down and then tipped gravel over them
there has been no escape since
text: The chap next door stopped me at the gate to tell me about his rabbits. They had been digging under the wire, he said, and heading straight for the vegetable patch at the bottom of the plot. Had he tried sinking the netting deeper? He had, and it made no odds, because they were still slipping out through some gap he had never managed to find. His daughter, who was listening, said he should lay a wide board flat on the ground, tight against the fence. It struck me as sound: an animal that digs goes at the foot of whatever stands in its way, and once it meets something hard underneath, it gives the job up. So they nailed the boards down and tipped gravel over the wood. Not one rabbit has got out since. He still laughs about it: he was planning a wall, and his daughter settled it with offcuts.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of taming existed at the same time
the first came about without any human intention
animals drew close to the camps for the food scraps
they bred on the spot alongside people
the second way rested on a choice made by keepers
the keepers held back the quiet animals and got rid of the fierce ones
this sorting produced bloodlines that do not occur in the wild
bones found in rubbish heaps bear witness to the first process
pens and tethers bear witness to the second
the first process yielded companions and the second yielded herds
text: Two ways of taming ran side by side long before anyone wrote anything down, and researchers still tell them apart. The first owed nothing to human intention. Animals drifted in towards the camps for the scraps, put up with the people who lived there, and bred where they stood, so that the sorting happened on its own. The second was deliberate. Keepers held back the quiet beasts, got rid of the ones that turned on them, and within a handful of generations had shaped bloodlines that exist nowhere in the wild. Bones dug out of old rubbish heaps tell the first story; pens and tethers tell the second. Specialists point out that one road led to companions and the other to herds. The two overlap, of course, since a creature that came near by chance is kept on purpose one evening.

units: the piece describes what a coat reveals
a plain shade hides the animal in a stretch of sand or grass
a coat marked with spots copies foliage pierced by light
those spots wipe out the outline of the animal
ruffled hair traps air against the skin
that hair keeps a body warm without weighing it down
swimmers wear a dense pelt that holds water off the skin
every coat also gives off a scent
a dog nosing at a trunk reads there that one of its own kind went by
newborns wear a down that a breath will shift
text: A coat tells a story, and the eye needs time to read it. There is the plain shade first, which melts an animal away into a stretch of open sand or dry grass. There is the dappled coat, whose scattered shadows copy foliage pierced by light and blur the line of the back. There is the rough, wind-tousled hair that traps air against the skin and keeps a body warm without weighing it down. Then there is the close fur of the swimmers, packed so tight that water runs off it and never reaches the skin underneath. Every coat gives off a scent as well, and that scent travels: a dog nosing at a tree trunk reads there that one of its own kind went by. Last of all comes the down of the newborn, so light that a breath will move it. Colour speaks to the eye, texture to the cold, scent to memory.

units: a team strung a fine net between two poles at the edge of a copse
the birds taken were measured and weighed and then let go again
one bird ringed the season before was caught again in the same place
that recapture allowed a comparison of mass from one season to the next
the bird had lost a marked amount of weight
the loss fitted a hard winter
the technician added two measurements to the protocol
she recorded wing length and the state of the plumage
the final report calls for lasting watch over the site
the equipment was left standing for the season to come
text: The ringing season opened with a fine net strung between two slender poles at the edge of a copse. Every bird taken from it was measured, weighed on a field balance and then let go again straight away. On the third evening a bird ringed the season before turned up in the very same net, which made it possible to set the mass of one season against that of the next. The loss of weight proved marked, and it matched a winter that had been hard. The technician widened the protocol on the spot: from then on she noted wing length and the state of the feathers as well, both of them signs of wear. By the close of the season the file held dozens of usable lines. The report concluded that the site deserved watching without a break, and the equipment was left standing exactly where it was.

units: a wall sheltered from the prevailing wind should be chosen
an exposed entrance lets rain in and chills the eggs
the support must be solid because a box that sways frightens the occupants
the entrance hole must stay narrow
a wide opening makes it easy for predators to get in
the box must be set beyond the reach of cats
no branch nearby should offer a foothold
the inside must not be lined because the occupants bring their own materials
damp padding rots the brood
a clean-out at the end of the season removes parasites that would harm the next clutch
text: Before you put up a nesting box, pick a wall that is sheltered from the prevailing wind, since an entrance left exposed takes in the rain and chills the eggs beneath. Fix the back panel to something thoroughly solid: a box that sways unsettles the birds inside, and they abandon it at the first alarm. Cut the entrance hole small, because a wide one makes life far too easy for predators. Set the whole thing beyond the reach of cats, at shoulder height at the very least, with no branch nearby that might offer a foothold. Do not line the inside, since the occupants bring their own materials and damp padding holds a wetness that rots the brood. Clean the cavity out once the season is over, because the parasites that build up in the debris will spoil the clutch that comes after.

units: walkers reported that the young ducks along a canal were vanishing
an association of naturalists looked into what was happening
the concrete slope kept the young from getting out of the water
the bread thrown by passers-by drew in rodents
those rodents were wrecking the nests
the local authority sank sloping wooden ramps into the water
the young can climb these ramps unaided
signs explain that bread does the birds harm
a later count found more young alive
those in charge hold that one season is not enough to conclude
text: For weeks, walkers along the banks of a town canal had been reporting that the duck broods were vanishing. An association of naturalists looked into it and came back with two causes. The concrete slope of the bank gave the ducklings nothing to climb, so they could not get out of the water at all, and the rats drawn in by the bread that passers-by throw were working their way through the nests. The local authority first sank wooden ramps into the water, set at a steep pitch, which the young can now climb unaided. Signs went up afterwards explaining that bread does the birds harm and feeds the rodents instead. A count taken when the warm weather came round again found more young alive than the year before. Those running the scheme are careful, though: one season proves nothing, and the watch goes on.
